data.title: Libya's NOC says 'unlawful' pipeline closure from Sharara oilfield to cut output by 350,000 bpd
data.description:
Nov 23 (Reuters) - Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said on Monday the closure of a valve on a pipeline from the Sharara oilfield, one of Libya's largest, by an "unlawful group" would result in the loss of around 350,000 barrels per day (bpd) of production.

A second pipeline, linking the Hamada field to the country's largest refinery, Zawiya, has also remained closed for more than two weeks, resulting in the loss of around 15,000 bpd, the NOC said, bringing Libya's total oil production losses to approximately 365,000 bpd.

The NOC said in October that an armed group had shut a valve on the main Hamada crude oil pipeline, halting flows. The Corporation said on Saturday that the forced closure of the Hamada oil pipeline had cost the country more than $30.8 million, renewing its condemnation of attacks on oil facilities.

Located ​in southwestern Libya, Sharara ​is operated ⁠by a joint venture of the state-owned NOC via Acacus oil company with Spain's Repsol, France's TotalEnergies, Austria's ​OMV and Norway's Equinor ( EQNR ).

Libyan oil output has been subject to repeated closures for political ​and technical reasons since the 2011 uprising against Muammar Gaddafi.

Oil production is Libya's main economic resource, representing ​approximately 90% ⁠of its economy.

(Reporting by Yomna Ehab; Editing by Tom Hogue and Lincoln Feast.)

data.title: AIPro Releases Free Version of 'VistaPro' AI Fire Early-Detection Software, Working with Existing CCTV
data.description:
Download requires no sign-up; basic features available with no time limit; includes 1 AI detection channel and 2 general monitoring channels

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AIPro, an AI video analytics company, has released a free version of VistaPro, its fire and smoke detection monitoring software. The release allows facility operators to use basic functions with their existing CCTV cameras and PCs, confirm whether the software suits their actual site, and then add features as needed.

The free version can be downloaded from the AIPro official website (www.aipro.ai/download) without registration or login. The basic functions provided free of charge have no usage time limit. Users connect existing CCTV cameras that support RTSP video streaming to an Intel-based Windows PC that meets the recommended specifications, and the software runs without a separate high-performance graphics card.

The free version supports a total of three channels: one AI fire detection channel and two general monitoring channels. The fire detection channel analyzes flames and smoke, and video from multiple cameras can be viewed on a single screen. Detection history, statistics, and automatic reporting are also provided.

Real-time video analysis is performed on the user's PC. Both the free version (Free) and the paid Pro plan require an internet connection for updates and version management. Before installation, users can check the recommended PC specifications and CCTV integration requirements on the website.

The free distribution is designed so that users can verify CCTV compatibility and fire and smoke detection in their actual operating environment, and determine the features and operating scale their facilities need.

AIPro recommends first trying the software in a single area where fire risk needs to be monitored. Because camera angles, lighting, and work conditions differ from site to site, the company explained that it is important to review detection results at different times of day and decide on the operating approach accordingly. AI analysis results are used by managers to judge on-site conditions and the need for a response.

Real-time alerts, email notifications, and fire and map-based monitoring are provided in the paid Pro plan. AI detection channels can be added as needed, and a Business plan is available for companies and organizations that operate more cameras or need closed-network or site-specific configurations. Users start with the basic functions and then choose whether to expand according to their operating scale and purpose.

AIPro is an AI video analytics company founded in 2020 by Professor Cheon-Su Park of Sungkyunkwan University. It has built experience applying video analytics technology in the field for public institutions, including supplying fire and wildfire detection software to the Korea Asset Management Corporation.

AIPro believes that even small stores, warehouses, and workshops can evaluate the feasibility of AI safety management using their existing equipment. Going forward, the company plans to continue research to enhance fire and smoke detection performance and reduce false alarms, while improving ease of use from installation to reviewing detection results and managing records.

data.title: ROI-AI bust hurts Chinese stocks far more than GDP: Manishi Raychaudhuri
data.description:
HONG KONG, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The AI boom turbocharged China's export machine. A bust might not tank GDP, but it would be very bad news for China's equity market.

China's AI export boom has become an increasingly important support for the country's growth. Its global trade surplus topped $1 trillion in the first 10 months of 2026, driven by AI-related demand and weak domestic consumption. But a global AI spending slowdown or tighter US tech curbs could test the limits of Beijing's strategy.

China's equity investors thus find themselves in a quandary: sluggish domestic consumption and mounting export uncertainty are weighing on the outlook.

That predicament has been exacerbated by recent developments, including China's weak October retail sales, factory output and housing data, and the announcement of enhanced US restrictions on AI chip sales to China in the wake of the Nvidia ( NVDA ) scandal.

Former CEO Jensen Huang, who was ousted from the chip giant on November 12 for having multiple alleged affairs including with a suspected Chinese spy, was a prominent advocate for looser export controls, arguing that strict bans would only accelerate China's drive for technological self-reliance. His departure suggests the most recent curbs may be just the beginning.

Combined with investors' growing concerns about AI profitability, this raises the risk of a slowdown in US AI spending.

The potential impact on China's GDP would be significant - but not straightforward.

HIT FROM BOTH SIDES

China's dependence on AI-related exports was underscored in the third quarter. Net exports contributed almost 40% of gross domestic product (GDP) growth, and within Chinese merchandise exports, AI and technology-related goods occupy centre stage. The share of these goods climbed rapidly from an average of 25% of total exports over the decade through early 2025 to 33% by August 2026.

That might suggest that an AI slowdown could hit China's economic growth hard, but when calculating GDP, it is net exports - the value remaining after subtracting imports from exports - that matters, rather than gross exports alone.

This is a critical distinction because China's AI export model is heavily reliant on imported components. According to FactSet data, imports of technology-related products have skyrocketed amid the AI boom, rising to 37% of total Chinese imports over the past 14 months, after hovering around 25%-27% in the first half of 2025.

Those imports would probably also decline if AI spending faltered, meaning China's net exports could remain relatively protected, and the hit to GDP growth could be contained.

THE REAL RISK

What may worsen, however, is the US effort to contain China's technological progress, and that could have significant market impacts.

US-China relations appeared to have improved considerably this year, at least until a few weeks ago.

The US extended its trade truce with China to January 10, postponing punitive tariffs originally scheduled to take effect on November 10. Beijing mirrored the US pause by suspending its retaliatory 24% tariff applied broadly to all US-origin imported goods, and extending rare-earth and critical-mineral export waivers.

The two presidents, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, have also met multiple times this year, most recently at last week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. The mood was positive, as they appeared to largely sidestep the AI trade issue.

But the question of technology sharing clearly remains a sore point that has gotten a lot more painful with the Nvidia ( NVDA ) drama. Xi notably called out "trade protectionism" at the summit following the US chip curb announcement.

Further deterioration in US-China ties, alongside a potential slowdown in AI capital spending, could increase pressure on Beijing to stimulate domestic consumption, an approach it has long resisted as it prioritises manufacturing and technology self-reliance.

Yet China may resist making significant changes if it views the threat to GDP growth as limited, as my analysis suggests may be the case.

That could prolong tough times for Chinese equity investors, as they may be caught between a slowing domestic economy and vulnerable exports.

SLIM PICKINGS

No sector bet seems to be working in Chinese stocks this year. The semiconductor, tech hardware and robotics companies represented in the Shanghai STAR50 index, such as Cambricon Technologies, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC) and Unitree Robotics , surged in the first half of 2026, only to collapse in the second half amid rising AI capex anxiety.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index, dominated by financials, consumers and industrials, and the mainland's CSI 300 Index , which is weighted toward technology hardware, financials, industrials and materials stocks, have performed no better.

China's domestic economy continues to be plagued by disorderly competition and declining margins, while technology exporters are now beleaguered by concerns about the robustness of their revenue.

In this environment, three areas stand out: policy-backed domestic champions, exporters with credible overseas supply chains, and selected biotech and drug-services companies that could benefit from surging global demand for specific molecules.

However, even here, the investment thesis is not always clear-cut. For example, market-leading household appliance, electric vehicle and battery manufacturers with overseas supply chains - such as Midea, Geely, BYD and CATL - could be relatively well positioned, yet most continue to face intense domestic competition, likely capping upside.

The situation could change, of course. Concerns about the health of the AI ecosystem could prove overblown. Or stringent US regulatory guardrails could inadvertently aid Chinese AI models. Absent such good fortune, however, an AI slowdown might simply harden Beijing's supply-side bias, leaving equity markets stuck.

(The views expressed here are those of Manishi Raychaudhuri, the founder and CEO of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd and the former head of Asia-Pacific equity research at BNP Paribas Securities.)

data.title: OpenAI scientist proposes industry AI limits tied to model intelligence metric
data.description:
Nov 22 (Reuters) - AI developers should adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use "perplexity" as a common metric for measuring AI progress across the industry, OpenAI's chief scientist said on Sunday in a proposal backed by CEO Sam Altman.

The proposal detailed by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a blog post was unveiled at a time of growing concern inside and outside the industry about the potential risks of AI's rapidly growing capabilities.

"I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone," Pachocki wrote.

Pachocki described perplexity as a model intelligence metric concerning how well a model predicts the next token - the basic unit of data - on average, and wrote that lower perplexity means better predictions.

Pachocki wrote that AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027, potentially accelerating progress more quickly than advances in monitoring and safety. Developers should commit to not cross agreed capability thresholds until new monitoring and safety mechanisms are in place, Pachocki said.

Pachocki advocated for an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, and defines what milestones must be met before that limit is exceeded.

Altman backed the proposal, saying in a post on X that the industry should seek agreement on common limits for AI development. Altman described Pachocki's essay as "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," and said such limits would help ensure safety and control.

(Reporting by Disha Mishra in Bengaluru; Editing by Will Dunham)

data.title: Beijing to bar young 'red-chip' firms from listing outside mainland China, sources say
data.description:
Nov 20 (Reuters) - China's securities watchdog has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip firms to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said, a move that tightens its control of capital raised offshore and could dent Hong Kong's IPO market.

Red-chip companies are registered abroad, mainly in tax havens, but control assets and businesses in China via equity ownership or contractual agreements.

The structure is favoured by Chinese startups, particularly tech firms, keen to raise capital in places like Hong Kong or New York to take advantage of more relaxed rules and deeper pools of funds available from foreign investors.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) has told law firm representatives in recent days that red-chip companies established after the introduction of new offshore listing rules in 2023 must be re-domiciled in China before they can list offshore, said the people.

The people declined to be identified as the regulatory guidance was confidential. The move is being reported for the first time by Reuters.

China and the US are competing fiercely to gain the upper hand in tech, particularly in AI and semiconductors, which has led to efforts by Chinese authorities to sharpen their scrutiny of technology, data and capital going outside its borders.

The CSRC did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Oversight of red-chip firms has gradually become stricter.

Prior to March 2023, Chinese companies employing overseas holding structures to raise capital abroad did not need regulatory approval. That changed with the advent of the new rules.

Then this year, the CSRC told Reuters in March that it was examining the "necessity and compliance" of red-chip structures, particularly those formed after March 2023.

Despite that warning, some red-chip IPO hopefuls and their advisors have been seeking approval to list outside the mainland without dismantling their existing structure and shifting their domicile back to China, one of the people said.

Most of those applicants failed to convince the regulator that a red-chip structure was necessary, prompting the tougher stance, the person added.

HONG KONG IPO MARKET COULD BE HURT

A drop-off in listings from red-chip firms is likely to hurt but not hobble Hong Kong, the top IPO destination for Chinese firms, which has seen business boom for the past 18 months.

Funds raised via IPOs in Hong Kong during the first 10 months of this year surged 84% from the same period last year to hit HK$404 billion ($52 billion), though the CSRC has slowed approvals of IPOs since September.

In addition to going slow on approvals for listings by AI, chip and humanoid robot firms after a market frenzy in those sectors, it has more broadly increased its scrutiny as markets have weakened.

Last year, one-fifth of 131 Hong Kong listings approved by the CSRC involved offshore holdings, the majority of which used a red-chip structure, according to Chinese law firm Han Kun.

So far this year, the CSRC has approved Hong Kong listings for just 6 red-chip companies, a sharp decline from 50 approved last year, according to data compiled by law firms and Reuters.

There were nearly 600 listing applications pending in Hong Kong at the end of October, official data showed.

Most of them are mainland Chinese firms though it was not clear how many are red chips given that the number includes applications that were filed confidentially.

There are, however, at least four active Hong Kong IPO applicants which have an offshore holding company structure for their mainland China businesses, according to a Reuters review of filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Any red-chip firms seeking to list in Hong Kong or New York could now face a long wait before coming to market due to the time and costs involved in becoming incorporated in China.

But some, like Chinese AI firm StepFun, have been working on shifting their domicile back to China to pave the way for a planned overseas listing, sources have said. StepFun did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Asked about news of the ban on red-chip firms listing outside mainland China, the Hong Kong bourse said it "welcomes issuers with a range of ownership structures, provided they meet all applicable regulatory requirements in Hong Kong and other relevant jurisdictions."

($1 = 7.8410 Hong Kong dollars)

(Reporting by Reuters staff; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

data.title: Trump to welcome investors at gala for his plunging meme coin
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump will headline his third meme coin gala on Sunday night at his country club outside Washington, DC, for top holders of the tokens, which were once worth about $75 each but are now valued at less than $1.

Less than 20 months after the first $TRUMP token gala set off a frenzy among 220 wealthy crypto holders vying for spots at the dinner with the president, interest has waned for the latest affair at the Trump National club in Sterling, Virginia.

Organizers indicated that 185 crypto wallets qualified for the dinner, although the leaderboard on the $TRUMP coin club website listed just 130 wallets when the contest concluded on November 16. Together, those listed wallets only held $8.6 million - a shadow of the $148 million listed for the first dinner in May 2025, when a time-weighted holding of $18.5 million grabbed the top seat.

According to the contest's website, the top 29 winners - which had the highest time-weighted holdings during the contest scoring period from September 30 to November 16 - will join a VIP reception with the president and receive a gift bag with Trump swag. The top four also get an 18-karat gold Trump-branded watch.

Trump and his family have monetized his brand through an array of equities and crypto ventures during his foray into politics.

More than half of the digital wallets publicly listed on the contest leaderboard for Sunday's dinner are tied directly to crypto exchanges that bar US-based users, indicating they are linked to foreign nationals, according to an analysis of blockchain data prepared for Reuters by the nonpartisan, nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen. 

Democratic leaders in the House and the Senate, where the party won a resounding victory in the midterm elections, have vowed to investigate what they say are unprecedented conflicts of interest posed by the Trump family's business dealings during Trump's presidency. They also say they plan to push for legislation that would ban such activities. 

The Trump Meme Coin project and the White House did not respond to requests for comment, although the Trump administration has long said the president's business interests are clean.

"Neither the President nor his family has ever engaged - or will ever engage - in conflicts of interest," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Reuters earlier this year. "President Trump proudly made the United States the crypto capital of the world through executive actions."

The Trump family's other crypto-connected equities and ventures have also fallen in value to record lows. Together, outside investors in their five main crypto and crypto-linked projects have lost more than $5 billion, according to a Reuters analysis. 

The Trump meme coin has earned the Trump family at least $635 million, according to the president's June financial disclosure statement. In total, the Trumps had earned at least $2.3 billion through April from their four main crypto ventures, including the meme coin.

The president's stake in a fifth crypto-linked venture, Trump Media & Technology Group ( DJT ), is worth about $430 million.

(Reporting by Michelle Conlin in New York; Editing by Sergio Non and Edmund Klamann)
